zanella: Arnaldo Zanella (b. 1949) is an Italian master glassmaker associated with the Murano glassmaking tradition. Born on Sant'Erasmo in the Venetian Lagoon, close to Murano, Zanella entered the world of Venetian glass at a young age and developed his craft among some of the leading glassmakers of his generation.

His early career was closely connected to Seguso Vetri d'Arte, where he worked alongside established figures including Alfredo Barbini, Angelo Seguso, Ermanno Nason and Pino Signoretto. Angelo Seguso selected Zanella as an assistant, giving him first-hand experience within one of Murano's important artistic glassmaking environments

In 1978, when renowned glass sculptor Pino Signoretto established his own furnace-studio, Zanella joined him. During this period he further developed his technical and artistic abilities while also attending evening drawing classes. This combination of furnace experience and formal drawing practice contributed to his development as an independent glass master.

A major step followed in 1985, when Zanella and several associates established the studio Andromeda. His work became particularly associated with brilliantly coloured and opalescent glass and with sculptural forms inspired by the natural world. Animals became an important part of his artistic vocabulary, with horses and birds among his most recognisable subjects.

From 1991, Zanella developed a long-standing professional association with Oscar Zanetti and Arte Zanetti Vetro. Zanetti Murano's own historical documentation includes Zanella among the masters connected with the glassworks, while contemporary secondary sources continue to document his association with the Zanetti workshop

Today, Zanella's work is particularly recognisable for its combination of traditional Murano craftsmanship, sculptural modelling and an enduring fascination with animal forms. His horses in particular form a distinctive part of his known body of work, appearing in transparent crystal as well as coloured and decorated glass. Signed examples from the 1980s and early 1990s are documented in the secondary market and auction record.
MURANIQ holds several works by Arnaldo Zanella in its private collection, including examples of his characteristic horse sculptures.
rosin: Loredano Rosin (1936–1992) was an Italian master glassmaker and sculptor whose work occupies a distinctive place in twentieth-century Murano glass. Born in Venice on 10 January 1936, he moved with his family to Murano in 1948, where his father Giovanni worked as a glassblower. Rosin entered the furnace at a young age and received his first training under master glassmaker Romano Zanetti, known as “Cocui Saor.”

Rosin developed within the traditional Murano apprenticeship system, progressing through different roles in the furnace while learning the techniques of Venetian glassmaking. Rather than concentrating on conventional blown glass, he became increasingly fascinated by solid glass, exploring its potential as a material for sculpture. This interest would become fundamental to his later artistic identity.

An important development came during the 1960s. Rosin briefly worked alongside master Ermanno Nason, and in 1965 began collaborating with Egidio Costantini's Fucina degli Angeli. Through this environment he participated in the translation of designs by internationally recognised artists into glass. Sources documenting this period associate the workshop with artists including Pablo Picasso, Marc Chagall, Max Ernst, Jean Arp and Jean Cocteau. The experience helped Rosin develop a more sculptural and three-dimensional approach to glass.

From 1968 to 1974, Rosin also worked as a master at Salviati & C. During these years he continued refining his ability to model substantial masses of hot glass, gradually moving away from traditional decorative production toward sculpture as an independent artistic form.

In 1975, Rosin established Vetreria Artistica Loredano Rosin, where he worked closely with his brother Dino Rosin. The studio gave him the freedom to pursue his own sculptural ideas and experiment with glass compositions and techniques that had become less common in contemporary Murano production.

One of the materials most strongly associated with Rosin is calcedonia (chalcedony) glass. By introducing metallic compounds into the molten glass, complex flowing striations and colour variations could be produced, reminiscent of natural minerals such as agate. Rosin combined these effects with his command of solid glass modelling to create highly individual sculptures.

The human figure became one of the defining subjects of his work. Heads, torsos, couples and stylised figures demonstrate his ability to transform a heavy mass of glass into forms that appear fluid, balanced and expressive. Animals and abstract sculptural forms also appear within his oeuvre. Surviving documented examples show his use of clear, smoked, coloured and calcedonia glass, often subsequently ground and polished by hand.

During the 1980s Rosin's work gained increasing international exposure, with exhibitions documented in the United States, Britain and Japan. His career was cut short by his death in 1992, leaving behind a body of work that illustrates the transition of Murano glass from traditional decorative craftsmanship toward autonomous sculptural expression.
MURANIQ holds works by Loredano Rosin in its private collection, including signed examples of his sculptural glass.
